explanations.explanation: The feature appears to detect boilerplate legal language—specifically, copyright and open‐source license headers (mostly Apache License 2.0) that include standard disclaimers and usage conditions.

It appears that the feature “lights up” on a particular subword‐chunk that nearly always occurs as the internal (or “middle”) fragment of compound words. In many examples—whether in scientific terms (as in complex chemical names), in programming and query language tokens (such as parts of “substr” or “computer”), or in mixed technical text—it is the central morphemic unit (for example, the “put” in “computer”) that is isolated. In short, the feature is sensitive to and conveys the semantic and structural importance of a frequently occurring internal substring that helps tie together otherwise disparate compound or morphologically complex words.

The feature appears to mark boilerplate legal header text—specifically, license and copyright statements (mostly Apache License v2 text with its associated disclaimers) that are commonly used at the top of source code files.

This feature flags standardized, formal “boilerplate” text that serves as document metadata or legal/official heading and citation information. It activates on texts containing fixed phrases, case identifiers, file names, court names, publication disclaimers, and similar structured administrative content.

This feature activates on text that poses arithmetic puzzles—particularly ones asking for remainders, modular outcomes, or related number‐theoretic properties (including digit extraction and greatest common factor/divisor problems). In short, it flags queries focused on division-based computations and modular arithmetic.

It’s a feature that reliably lights up on technical “code‐style” text—when the model sees structured markup, configuration metadata, identifiers, version strings, and hash-like tokens (the kinds of patterns you find in HTML, schema definitions, project config files, and code comments), this feature is activated.

It appears that this feature “lights up” when the model is parsing and manipulating mathematical or algebraic expressions—that is, when it’s performing structured, symbolic reasoning (e.g. solving equations, factoring numbers, and defining variables) within the context of formal math problems.
The feature seems to specialize in detecting negation cues—especially contracted forms like “don’t” and “isn’t”—that signal skepticism or denial in informal, opinionated language.

It appears that the feature is attuned to spotting and encoding structured, enumerative elements—tokens that mark numbered lists, categorical subitems, or reference-style annotations within dense, technical or scientific prose.

It appears that this feature has learned to “light‐up” on relational or linking words—the small connectors (often prepositions like “of” or verbs such as “use”) that signal an association between an entity and its property, parameter, or component. In many of these high‐activation examples (whether legal descriptions, technical setup instructions, programming code, or financial explanations), the feature is triggered when the text shifts into a mode of specifying relationships or attributes (for example, linking a value to an environment or a property to an object). In short, the feature represents the abstract notion of relational “glue” in structured, explanatory text that marks the connection between a subject and its modifiers or arguments.

It detects blocks of legal boilerplate—copyright notices and open‐source license texts (with version numbers, warranty disclaimers, and redistribution terms) as commonly found in source code comments.

It appears this feature “lights up” on tokens that serve as emphatic or conclusive discourse markers—words and proper‐names used in emotionally charged or summary statements (for example, exclamatory names, final “too,” “respectively,” “etc.”, etc.) that signal a shift into a heightened, definitive, or summarizing tone regardless of domain.

It detects text segments that look like formal legal citation and docket metadata—that is, fragments of court‐document headers (abbreviated case names, dates, docket numbers, court and judge identifiers) common to published legal opinions and filings.

It seems this feature is sensitive to the “head‐parts” of salient, often proper–noun or headline–like words. In each instance the model lights up on the opening syllable or fragment (e.g. “Fel” in Felicity, “Don” in Don’t, “Buck,” “H,” “Har,” “Mar”)—a pattern common to names, titles, or branded terms that signal the key entity or topic. In short, the feature appears to mark the beginnings of important or content–defining terms in a text.

The feature appears to be sensitive to segments of text that act like “headers” or “title‐style” passages—that is, it strongly activates on key proper nouns and domain‐specific keywords used to label institutions, products, events, or technical entities. In short, it detects when a text is formatted to convey high-level, structured identifiers and thematic descriptors (for example, names, design elements, and key industry terms) that summarize or define the subject area.

This feature appears to detect and emphasize conditional statements or clauses—the “if‐contexts” in which a condition, alternative, or ideal scenario is being specified. In other words, it activates strongly when the text is marking a branch in reasoning or instructions, as when the writer is stipulating “if … then …” or “ideally …”, framing contingency or recommendation.

It’s a “structured‐text” or formatting detector—that is, the feature fires when the model sees tokens typical of non‐plain language content (markup headers, code comments, file paths, special punctuation and mixed or non‐ASCII symbols) that signal technical or structured text rather than ordinary prose.

It appears that the feature is strongly activated by boilerplate legal text—specifically, license header blocks (copyright notices, open‐source license declarations, and associated legal disclaimers) that are common in source code files.

It appears to be a feature that “fires” on boilerplate, metadata‐style text – the kind of standardized legal, corporate, and interface copy (e.g. copyright notices, registration details, privacy policy prompts, and browser support banners) commonly found on websites and in system messages.

This feature appears to signal the presence of standardized source‐code boilerplate—segments that include project metadata such as license and copyright notices, structured header comments, import/include directives, and other fixed-format file annotations—that are common across various programming languages and code files.
